explanation: No single pattern. Strongest on a mid-name fragment in a paper's author list ('Haji'). Also fires on the 'title' key after YAML author lists in arXiv-style metadata, on '");' closing "License" in license headers, and on assorted code, subtitle-timestamp and name fragments. Mid and weak hits look random.

Fires on tokens inside multi-word technical or scientific terms, mostly in methods sections. Examples are 'and' linking paired method names ('univariate and multivariate', 'Funnel plots and Egger'), 'root'/'of' in 'root mean square'/'region of interest', and word pieces of technical words ('Doud', 'ivariate'). It also fires on assorted code and config tokens (typedef, 'encoding:', compiler flags). Ordinary prose barely activates it.

A mixture. Fires on library and import paths in code (the 'memory' in #include <memory>, '.com' in Go "github.com/..." imports) and on subword fragments in the middle of names and rare words (Hernan-DE-z, T-sim-is, Med-line, ureteros-copy). It also fires on LaTeX \cap and on scattered code tokens.

Fires on the first piece of a word that the tokenizer splits up. Most often this is the leading byte of a broken multi-byte CJK or Devanagari character, or a lone word-initial letter of a non-English or foreign word (' f'izesse, ' F'útbol, ' G'ypsies, ' k'ündigt, ' w'ettig, ' N'albari). Whole common English words are near zero.

Mostly weak and unfocused. The strongest hits are in MATLAB code with % comments: the assignment ' =' in 'R = roots(...)' and ']' in '[OUT,OFFS]'. Everything else (about 20-37%) is scattered: chemical-name fragments, Chinese characters, 'the', punctuation.

Two jobs. (1) Quote and string-delimiter tokens in code, especially around SQL query strings in PHP or Python and HTML or JS attributes ("'");", '="post', ' "main', 'method: "'). (2) Digits and decimal points in statistical values in biomedical abstracts, such as the '5' or '.' in 'P < 0.05' and in confidence intervals.

A mixture of boilerplate and header contexts. These include '.com' in URLs, 'District'/'COURT' in court captions ("Court of Appeals, Second District", "UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT"), 'village' in gazetteer stubs, and words in license or generated-file headers ('AUTHORS', 'futile', 'eslint-disable'). It also fires on dates, '======' separators and code tokens.

Fires on backslash tokens. These include namespace and path separators (PHP 'Doctrine\ORM\', '@ORM\', Windows registry 'Software\KeyName', 'HKLM\'), escape sequences ('\n', '\r'), doc-comment commands ('\class'), and the escaped ' \[' before inline citations like [@B1]. Strongest on separators and pre-citation backslashes; mid-level on other backslashes and template braces.

Fires on the first or a middle subword fragment of a word the tokenizer splits up. Strongest on the prefix 'unt' (untimely, untangle, untold, Untuk). Also fires on fragments of rare, technical or foreign words and names (lymph-ok-ines, N-au-voo, Ay-od-hya, eup-hor-ic, selen-oc-ysteine). Whole common words are near zero.

A mixture. It fires on opening quotation marks before a scare-quoted word or phrase (a “puzzle adventure”, the "cannon fodder", my "hollow list"), on fragments of citation keys ('eh'/'er' in ijerph or ehp references), and on verb fragments in Scandinavian and Dutch ('skjer', 'vindt', 'gjøre', 'Helt'). Other words are scattered.

No clear common feature. Fires on head-noun or mid-word pieces in fairly formal text (Per-man-ently, birth-place, car-box-y, equ-inoxes, finalist, conversion, missile), on CJK characters in Japanese and Chinese news, and on assorted function words. It is hard to predict from one rule.

Fires almost only on a '0' digit inside a long run of zeros (zero-padded or fixed-width numbers like '0000000'). Every other example is very weak (about 10% or less): ' from' in JS import statements, ':' in 'android:' XML attributes, and 'System' in C# using lines.

Several unrelated triggers. These are the ' *' starting the first line of a /** doc-comment at the top of a source file (PHP or Java headers), 'localhost' in URLs, the curly-apostrophe "’s" in "That’s", 'Lumpur' after 'Kuala', and URL or package path parts ('/TR', '.SerializedName', 'Copyright' in assembly attributes).

Mostly fires on tokens in passages that introduce a named person. These include the pronoun or comma right after the name in bio or interview intros ('In this podcast, he discusses', 'Co-Producer of Beyond Elections, talks') and subword pieces of the person's surname (Gr-uber, Dress-ler, G-ilm-our). A few unrelated code tokens also fire (RewriteRule, datomic ' :as', django '.generic').
